title: Section 2: Smoothing, Regression, State-Space Models and HMMs
text:
This section covers models for forecasting and for structure that changes over time. Exponential smoothing is the simplest state-space model. Regression adds explanatory terms such as harmonics, indicator variables and count-data models. The Kalman filter treats a quantity like a level or a regression coefficient as an unobserved state that moves over time. Hidden Markov models do the same for a discrete state, so the series switches between regimes.
I used the regression material in Project 3 (a negative-binomial model for withdrawals) and the state-space material in Project 4 (a time-varying beta). The tutorials here compare five forecasting methods on Eskom’s EAF, then build a hidden Markov model from first principles and test whether its regime lengths behave as the model assumes.

title: Section 2: Smoothing, Regression, State-Space Models and HMMs

Checking the code


Code
# Check 1: the forward log-likelihood must equal a brute-force sum over every state path (T = 6, m = 2)
set.seed(1); xs <- rnorm(6, 0, 2)
mu_t <- c(0, 3); sg_t <- c(1, 1.5); A_t <- matrix(c(.9, .1, .2, .8), 2, byrow = TRUE); d_t <- c(.5, .5)
brute <- sum(apply(expand.grid(rep(list(1:2), 6)), 1, function(p) {
  pr <- d_t[p[1]] * dnorm(xs[1], mu_t[p[1]], sg_t[p[1]])
  for (t in 2:6) pr <- pr * A_t[p[t - 1], p[t]] * dnorm(xs[t], mu_t[p[t]], sg_t[p[t]])
  pr
}))
diff_fw <- abs(hmm_forward(xs, mu_t, sg_t, A_t, d_t)$loglik - log(brute))

# Check 2: simulate a 3-state HMM with known parameters, then recover them
sim_hmm <- function(nT, mu, sg, A, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed); m <- length(mu); s <- integer(nT); s[1] <- 2L
  for (t in 2:nT) s[t] <- sample.int(m, 1, prob = A[s[t - 1], ])
  list(s = s, x = rnorm(nT, mu[s], sg[s]))
}
mu_s <- c(54, 62, 70); sg_s <- c(2.5, 2.5, 2); A_s <- matrix(c(.93, .07, 0, .04, .92, .04, 0, .08, .92), 3, byrow = TRUE)
sm <- sim_hmm(232, mu_s, sg_s, A_s)
fs <- fit_hmm(sm$x, 3, nstart = 5)
acc_dec <- mean(viterbi(sm$x, fs$mu, fs$sg, fs$A, fs$delta) == sm$s)       # share of weeks decoded correctly
mono <- all(diff(fs$lls) > -1e-8)                                           # EM must never decrease the likelihood

fits <- map(2:4, function(m) fit_hmm(y, m)); names(fits) <- 2:4
ll1 <- sum(dnorm(y, mean(y), sqrt(mean((y - mean(y))^2)), log = TRUE))      # single Gaussian, for reference

              k = c(2, (2:4)^2 + 2 * (2:4) - 1)) |>                          # initial dist + transitions + means + sds

# Optional cross-check against the depmixS4 package (uses its own starting values, so local optima can differ)
if (requireNamespace("depmixS4", quietly = TRUE)) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(depmixS4))        # attach so its logLik method is registered
  set.seed(1)
  dm  <- depmix(eaf ~ 1, data = data.frame(eaf = y), nstates = m_best, family = gaussian())
  dmf <- depmixS4::fit(dm, verbose = FALSE)                # explicit namespace, since tidyverse has no fit()
  ll_dm <- as.numeric(logLik(dmf))
}


converged at iteration 71 with logLik: -535.8169 


The depmixS4 package reaches a log-likelihood of -535.82 against -532.73 for my implementation (a difference of -3.09).
Limitations. EM finds local optima, so I use several starts. The model treats the Gaussian state-conditional distribution as fixed within a regime, but EAF has a trend and an annual cycle, so regimes partly absorb them. A hidden Markov model is therefore a description of regimes, not a causal account, and the number of regimes depends on the criterion used.

title: Project 1: Detailed Analysis
text:
Understanding and forecasting the volatility of emerging market currencies remains a central challenge in empirical finance, particularly for the South African Rand (ZAR) under conditions of shifting global liquidity and domestic macroeconomic sensitivity. This study investigates whether domestic investor attention, proxied by South African search interest in the rand via Google Trends, carries predictive information regarding next-week ZAR/USD volatility beyond the predictive content already embedded in past returns.
To appropriately capture conditional heteroskedasticity and fat-tailed return dynamics, the analysis employs a Student-t GARCH(1,1) specification augmented with a lagged Google Trends regressor in the conditional variance equation. The underlying likelihood function is custom-coded with strict non-negativity constraints imposed directly on the parameter space, and its empirical performance is benchmarked against standard GARCH, GJR-GARCH, and EGARCH models. Evaluation is conducted through a multi-faceted framework comprising a boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test, out-of-sample QLIKE loss evaluations against high-frequency realised variance measures, Granger causality tests, and rigorous robustness checks. Additionally, a Monte Carlo power study is implemented to determine the precise statistical power and detectable effect sizes afforded by the sample size. The complete set of numerical findings and diagnostic evaluations is compiled in Section 4.8.

title: Project 1: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.1 Model
Let r_t be the weekly log return (%). The GARCH-X model is

r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t,\qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} t_\nu \text{ (unit variance)},
 
\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha\,\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta\,\sigma_{t-1}^2 + \delta\,x_{t-1}.

Positivity. \sigma_t^2>0 for all t requires \omega>0, \alpha,\beta,\delta\ge 0 and x\ge 0, which is why x is scaled to [0,1]. Standard software does not impose \delta \ge 0, so I code the likelihood myself with box constraints.
Stationarity. Covariance stationarity requires \alpha+\beta<1. The half-life of a shock is \ln 0.5/\ln(\alpha+\beta) weeks, and a sustained one-unit move in x changes long-run variance by \delta/(1-\alpha-\beta).
Timing. Using x_{t-1} means the regressor is known at the forecast origin, which avoids look-ahead bias.
Errors. Student-t innovations capture heavy tails. Estimation is by quasi-maximum likelihood, since the t assumption may be wrong (Bollerslev and Wooldridge 1992).

GJR-GARCH (Glosten, Jagannathan, and Runkle 1993)

title: Project 1: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.3 Inference and evaluation
In-sample testing: The likelihood-ratio test statistic is formulated as \mathrm{LR} = 2(\ell_{X} - \ell_{0}), where the restricted null model is estimated by fixing \delta = 0. Because this parameter restriction sits squarely on the boundary of the admissible parameter space under the null, the asymptotic distribution does not follow a standard \chi^2_1 distribution; instead, it collapses to an equal mixture distribution \frac{1}{2}\chi^2_0 + \frac{1}{2}\chi^2_1 (Self and Liang 1987). Both naive and boundary-corrected p-values are reported.
Out-of-sample evaluation: Predictive accuracy is evaluated using an expanding-window scheme generating one-step-ahead conditional variance forecasts h_{t+1\vert{}t}, initiating evaluation after 60% of the sample has elapsed. The forecast target is weekly realized variance RV_t = \sum r_d^2, which serves as a substantially more efficient proxy than squared weekly returns. Models are evaluated using the robust QLIKE loss function:

L(h,RV)=\ln h + RV/h,

which maintains robust ranking properties even in the presence of noisy volatility proxies (Patton 2011). Loss differentials d_t = L^{\text{base}}_t - L^{\text{alt}}_t are evaluated using a Diebold-Mariano regression on a constant with Newey-West heteroskedasticity-autocorrelation-consistent standard errors (Diebold and Mariano 1995; Newey and West 1987), utilizing Student-t critical values based on degrees of freedom m-1. A positive mean differential favors the alternative specification.
Granger causality tests:Bivariate Granger causality tests between weekly search changes and log realized variance are conducted across multiple lag lengths, adjusting for family-wise error rates using the Holm procedure (Granger 1969).
Monte Carlo power analysis To evaluate empirical test sensitivity, artificial series are simulated from the fitted null model, augmented with artificial attention effects of known magnitudes, recording the empirical rejection frequency of the boundary-corrected LR test at the 5% significance level across various effect sizes to determine minimum detectable effects.

title: Project 1: Detailed Analysis
text:
4.1 Estimation by constrained maximum likelihood

# Conditional variance recursion; p = (mu, omega, alpha, beta, delta, nu)
gx_filter <- function(p, y, x) {
  e <- y - p[1]; n <- length(y); h <- numeric(n)
  h[1] <- var(y)                                                      # start at the sample variance
  for (t in 2:n) h[t] <- p[2] + p[3] * e[t-1]^2 + p[4] * h[t-1] + p[5] * x[t]
  h
}

# Negative log-likelihood with unit-variance Student-t innovations
garchx_nll <- function(p, y, x) {
  if (p[3] + p[4] >= 0.9999) return(1e10)                             # penalty enforces alpha + beta < 1
  h <- gx_filter(p, y, x); z <- (y - p[1]) / sqrt(h); nu <- p[6]
  ll <- lgamma((nu + 1) / 2) - lgamma(nu / 2) - 0.5 * log(pi * (nu - 2)) -
        0.5 * log(h) - (nu + 1) / 2 * log1p(z^2 / (nu - 2))           # density of sigma * z
  out <- -sum(ll)
  if (is.finite(out)) out else 1e10
}

# Box-constrained fit; delta_zero = TRUE pins delta at 0 (the null model)
# Multi-start box-constrained fit; delta_zero = TRUE fixes delta at 0 and drops it from the search
fit_gx <- function(y, x, delta_zero = FALSE, par0 = NULL, n_start = 4) {
  v <- var(y); m <- mean(y)
  nm    <- c("mu", "omega", "alpha", "beta", "delta", "nu")
  lower <- c(-Inf, 1e-8, 0, 0, 0, 2.05)               # nonnegativity gives h > 0
  upper <- c(Inf, Inf, 1, 1, Inf, 200)
  free  <- if (delta_zero) c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6) else 1:6  # parameters actually optimised

  full <- function(q) { p <- numeric(6); p[free] <- q; if (delta_zero) p[5] <- 0; p }
  obj  <- function(q) garchx_nll(full(q), y, x)

  # Fixed grid of starts: GARCH-like, ARCH-like, mixed, attention-heavy
  grid <- list(
    c(m, 0.10 * v, 0.10, 0.80, 0.01 * v, 8),
    c(m, 0.50 * v, 0.25, 0.00, 0.10 * v, 4),
    c(m, 0.30 * v, 0.10, 0.40, 0.50 * v, 6),
    c(m, 0.10 * v, 0.15, 0.00, 1.00 * v, 4))
  starts <- c(if (!is.null(par0)) list(par0), grid[seq_len(n_start)])   # warm start first, if given

  fits <- lapply(starts, function(s) {
    s <- pmin(pmax(s, lower), upper)                  # keep each start inside the bounds
    tryCatch(optim(s[free], obj, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = lower[free], upper = upper[free]), error = function(e) NULL)
  })
  fits <- Filter(Negate(is.null), fits)
  ok   <- Filter(function(o) o$convergence == 0 && o$value < 1e9, fits)   # converged and finite
  pool <- if (length(ok)) ok else fits
  best <- pool[[which.min(vapply(pool, function(o) o$value, numeric(1)))]] # keep the best optimum
  list(par = setNames(full(best$par), nm), ll = -best$value, conv = best$convergence)
}

gx_next <- function(p, y, x, x_next) {
  e <- y - p[1]; h <- gx_filter(p, y, x); n <- length(y)
  unname(p[2] + p[3] * e[n]^2 + p[4] * h[n] + p[5] * x_next)
}

# Boundary-corrected LR test of delta = 0; each fit is also seeded from the other's solution
gx_test <- function(y, x) {
  f1 <- fit_gx(y, x)
  f0 <- fit_gx(y, x, TRUE, par0 = f1$par)
  f1 <- fit_gx(y, x, par0 = replace(f0$par, 5, 0.01 * var(y)))
  if (f1$ll < f0$ll) f1 <- f0                                        # delta = 0 is feasible, so LR >= 0
  LR <- 2 * (f1$ll - f0$ll)
  tibble(delta = unname(f1$par[5]), LR = LR,
         p = if (LR <= 0) 1 else 0.5 * pchisq(LR, 1, lower.tail = FALSE))   # 0.5 chi0 + 0.5 chi1
}

# Expanding-window forecasts from the hand-coded GARCH and GARCH-X
roll_gx <- function(y, x, s0) {
  n <- length(y); h0 <- h1 <- rep(NA_real_, n); p0 <- p1 <- NULL
  for (t in s0:(n - 1)) {
    f0 <- fit_gx(y[1:t], x[1:t], TRUE,  par0 = p0)                  # baseline: delta = 0
    f1 <- fit_gx(y[1:t], x[1:t], FALSE, par0 = p1)                  # GARCH-X
    p0 <- f0$par; p1 <- f1$par                                      # warm starts for the next origin
    if (f0$conv == 0) h0[t + 1] <- gx_next(f0$par, y[1:t], x[1:t], x[t + 1])
    if (f1$conv == 0) h1[t + 1] <- gx_next(f1$par, y[1:t], x[1:t], x[t + 1])
  }
  tibble(h0, h1)
}

# Same scheme for the GJR benchmark via rugarch (no regressor)
roll_gjr <- function(y, s0) {
  h <- rep(NA_real_, length(y))
  for (t in s0:(length(y) - 1)) {
    f <- tryCatch(fit_garch(y[1:t], model = "gjrGARCH"), error = function(e) NULL)   # skip failed refits
    if (!is.null(f)) h[t + 1] <- as.numeric(sigma(ugarchforecast(f, n.ahead = 1)))^2
  }
  h
}

text:
4.7 Power: what could this sample have detected?
Because failure to reject a null hypothesis can stem either from a true absence of an effect or from insufficient statistical power in a modest sample, a Monte Carlo power study is conducted to evaluate test sensitivity. Simulating artificial series from the fitted null model augmented with artificial attention effects of varying magnitudes allows us to record the empirical rejection frequency of the boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test at the five percent significance level. This procedure establishes the minimum detectable effect size required to achieve eighty percent statistical power, ensuring that a non-rejection is interpreted correctly against the backdrop of sample size limitations rather than misconstrued as definitive proof of no relationship.


Code
p_null <- g0$par                                          # fitted null model

# Simulate from the null plus an added attention effect v (variance units)
sim_gx <- function(n, p, x, v) {
  nu <- p[6]; z <- rt(n, nu) * sqrt((nu - 2) / nu)        # unit-variance t shocks
  h <- e <- numeric(n); h[1] <- var(y); e[1] <- sqrt(h[1]) * z[1]
  for (t in 2:n) { h[t] <- p[2] + p[3] * e[t-1]^2 + p[4] * h[t-1] + v * x[t]; e[t] <- sqrt(h[t]) * z[t] }
  p[1] + e
}

title: Reflective commentary
text:
At the start of this module, I approached time series modelling predominantly as a mechanical fitting exercise: selecting a model family, estimating parameters, comparing information criteria, and declaring a winner. However, the trajectory of the four projects fundamentally reshaped this perspective. By the conclusion of the coursework, my core inquiry had shifted from asking whether a model fit to questioning whether the underlying data could support any model at all, and critically, what inferences I would be entitled to draw if it could not. This reflective commentary traces that evolution through four pivotal moments where my initial expectations proved mistaken.
Project 2 investigated whether Eskom’s energy availability and the JSE All Share index share cyclical dynamics. The squared coherence function registered a prominent peak of 0.67 at a period of seven weeks, which immediately presented itself as the natural headline finding. Yet, this interpretation overlooked fundamental statistical properties: (1) coherence is estimated via a smoothed periodogram characterized by few effective degrees of freedom, and (2) my analytical process involved searching across a broad spectrum of frequencies to isolate the maximum value. A standard single-frequency critical value fails to account for this multiple-testing search space.
To rigorously address this, I simulated the null distribution of the maximum statistic. The observed peak yielded a family-wise p-value of 0.127, precluding any rejection of the null. Although one of six robustness alternatives did reject, I transparently reported that result alongside its context. Furthermore, because the dataset spanned only approximately 231 weeks, the inherent sample size strictly constrained statistical power; consequently, I framed the conclusion as suggestive and underpowered rather than as definitive evidence of an absence of relationship.
This marked the module’s turning point where methodological precision regarding uncertainty superseded the desire for a clean, affirmative answer. This project also underscored the vital importance of rigorous code auditing. My custom coherence routine diverged from spec.pgram by roughly 1.6 \times 10^{-2} until I successfully aligned the internal demeaning procedures. While the discrepancy was minor, it would have remained entirely undetected without direct comparative verification.
In Section 1, I implemented the Whittle likelihood for an ARMA(1,1) process and evaluated parameter recovery using simulated data. Initial specifications with \phi = 0.6 and \theta = -0.4 produced highly unstable estimates. The underlying cause was structural: when the autoregressive and moving average roots lie in close proximity, the two terms nearly cancel out, rendering the likelihood surface exceptionally flat in that direction. The estimator was functioning precisely as designed; rather, the flaw lay in my simulation parameterisation. By adjusting the true parameters to \phi = 0.7 and \theta = 0.5, where the roots are cleanly separated, parameter recovery behaved sensibly. This investigation demonstrated that a simulation study merely illustrates where a method functions, and the specific parameter values selected actively dictate what insights are acquired. Consequently, I now treat parameter selection as an integral component of the analytical design, explicitly detailing its rationale in the write-up.
Project 3 was originally intended to examine pension withdrawals under South Africa’s Two-Pot retirement system, yet no public time series of actual withdrawal counts existed. Rather than forcing an artificial proxy, I constructed a bespoke simulation calibrated directly against published SARS figures while analyzing Google Trends data separately via a quasi-Poisson framework, ensuring both components remained meticulously distinguished and labelled. The simulation provided a reliable sandbox to verify that my hand-coded Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) algorithm for the negative-binomial model successfully recovered known parameters. Simultaneously, the Google Trends data illustrated the empirical nature of a real yet indirect behavioural signal. Formulating the methodological justification for this dual-pronged design reinforced a broader lesson: stating data limitations plainly and honestly equips the reader with a sound basis to trust every other facet of the analysis.
Project 4 utilized a state-space regression model featuring time-varying coefficients. To formally test whether the coefficients genuinely varied over time, I compared it against a constant-coefficient specification using a likelihood-ratio test. Because the null hypothesis restricts a variance parameter to zero, sitting squarely on the boundary of the parameter space, the conventional \chi^2 asymptotic reference distribution is invalid. The correct theoretical reference is instead an equal mixture of \chi^2_0 and \chi^2_1 distributions. Additionally, I discovered that the likelihood value of the diffuse-drift model was incomparable with the other specifications; consequently, I restricted formal likelihood comparisons strictly to the nested pair and evaluated the broader model set via out-of-sample forecasts validated through a Diebold-Mariano test. Notably, neither Kalman filter model outperformed an expanding-window OLS benchmark out of sample (yielding a best Mean Squared Error ratio of 1.000, which collapses identically to OLS), confirming that the added model flexibility yielded zero forecasting gains. Both lessons stem from a single essential habit: rigorously verifying that two numerical metrics actually measure the exact identical quantity before attempting a comparison.
Reflecting on the workflow, I would prioritize establishing the evaluation framework prior to constructing the model architecture. Across several projects, I wrote the estimation code first and devised the validation strategy afterward. For instance, the true ARMA(1,1) parameters for the Whittle study were only locked down after the initial recovery run failed, necessitating a complete re-run of the entire simulation pipeline. Furthermore, I would maintain contemporaneous logs detailing the rationale behind each analytical decision, as compiling the retrospective journal vividly exposed how easily nuanced decisions are forgotten when reconstructed later. In Section 2, the hidden Markov model inherently implies geometric state durations. My empirical duration check revealed observed run lengths closely mirroring geometric expectations, for example, 7.2 weeks against a theoretical 7.3 weeks for regime 3, with only regime 1 showing a noticeable divergence (10.7 against 14.0 weeks). While the data offered no definitive evidence to reject the Markov assumption, the total sample of 21 observed runs remains too sparse to be conclusive. Moving forward, I am keen to explore semi-Markov formulations, which allow the duration distribution to be modelled explicitly.
Ultimately, the module did not alter my conviction that rigorous modelling matters; rather, it redefined what I consider rigorous. A model that achieves a strong statistical fit merely marks the commencement of the analytical work. The true substance lies in rigorously determining what the data can and cannot substantiate, and articulating those boundaries clearly so that independent scrutiny is genuinely possible.

title: Project 1: GARCH-X
text:
Section and topic
Part 1: Volatility modelling (ARCH and GARCH)


Type of project
Exploration and simulation study, with a hand-coded likelihood


Data used
Daily USD/ZAR close (Yahoo Finance, USDZAR=X) aggregated to weeks, and weekly Google Trends interest for “dollar rand” in South Africa. Period: 21 Nov 2021 to 18 Oct 2026 (257 weeks). Both series are public and aggregate, so no personal data and no POPIA consent issue.


Methods used
Student-t GARCH(1,1) with a lagged search term in the variance equation (GARCH-X), estimated by constrained quasi-maximum likelihood. GJR-GARCH and EGARCH benchmarks. Boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test. Out-of-sample QLIKE against realised variance (HAC and block-bootstrap tests). Granger tests with Holm correction. Monte Carlo power study.

title: Project 2: Detailed Analysis
text:
Investigating the dynamic interactions between national energy reliability and broader macroeconomic equity performance is vital for understanding systemic economic vulnerabilities in developing markets, particularly given South Africa’s structural reliance on power generation stability. This study examines whether Eskom’s Energy Availability Factor (EAF) and JSE All Share index returns move together at specific frequencies, and whether either series exhibits lead-lag dynamics relative to the other. To capture these frequency-domain relationships, the analysis estimates the cross-spectrum using a custom-coded coherence estimator validated directly against R’s spec.pgram routine.
Statistical significance is evaluated through a dual-testing framework comparing results against conventional pointwise F-thresholds as well as a rigorous family-wise threshold derived by simulating independent series with identical autocorrelation structures. Furthermore, a simulation study verifies that the methodological pipeline successfully recovers a known lead-lag relationship, while comprehensive robustness checks assess sensitivity to varying bandwidths, differencing transformations, and subsample periods. The full suite of empirical numbers and detailed results is compiled in Section 4.8.

title: Project 2: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.1 Cross-spectral estimators
Let X_j and Y_j represent the discrete Fourier transforms of the demeaned series evaluated at fundamental frequencies f_j = j/n. The raw cross-periodogram is defined as I_{xy}(f_j) = X_j\overline{Y_j}/n. Smoothing via a modified Daniell kernel of half-width m yields smoothed spectral density estimates \hat f_{xx}, \hat f_{yy}, and cross-spectral density \hat f_{xy}. Squared coherence and phase are subsequently calculated as:
\hat\rho^2_{xy}(f)=\frac{|\hat f_{xy}(f)|^2}{\hat f_{xx}(f)\,\hat f_{yy}(f)},\qquad \hat\phi(f)=\arg \hat f_{xy}(f).
Under this sign convention, if y represents x delayed by k weeks, the phase satisfies \hat\phi(f) = 2\pi f k, implying that \hat\phi/(2\pi f) estimates the temporal lead of x over y. Simulation checks confirm this sign convention.

title: Project 2: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.2 Two thresholds
Pointwise evaluation: The Daniell smoothing window implies equivalent degrees of freedom L = 1/\sum w_i^2. Under the null hypothesis of zero coherence at an individual frequency, the sample squared coherence exceeds F_{2,2L-2}(\alpha) / (L - 1 + F_{2,2L-2}(\alpha)) with probability \alpha (Shumway and Stoffer 2025). Across roughly n/2 Fourier frequencies, multiple testing dictates that approximately \alpha n/2 exceedances will occur purely by chance, rendering isolated pointwise crossings unreliable.
Family-wise evaluation: To control family-wise error rates, an autoregressive model is fitted to each series, and independent series with identical autocorrelation structures are simulated repeatedly. The maximum coherence across all frequencies is recorded for each simulation, establishing the 95th percentile of these maxima as the rigorous family-wise critical threshold. The proportion of simulations yielding a maximum exceeding the empirically observed peak defines the family-wise p-value.

title: Project 2: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.3 Choices fixed beforehand
Smoothing bandwidth is fixed at m = 3 (averaging seven adjacent Fourier frequencies), pointwise significance is set at \alpha = 1\%, family-wise confidence is set at 95%, and simulation replications are fixed at 2000. Variations in bandwidth, differencing transformations, and subsample periods are treated strictly as robustness checks rather than exploratory specification searches.

title: Project 2: Detailed Analysis
text:
4.1 Estimators: hand-coded and validated

# Modified Daniell weights of half-width m (2m+1 terms summing to 1)
daniell_w <- function(m) c(0.5, rep(1, 2 * m - 1), 0.5) / (2 * m)

# Circular smoothing of a complex vector
smooth_circ <- function(v, w) {
  complex(real = as.numeric(stats::filter(Re(v), w, circular = TRUE)),
          imaginary = as.numeric(stats::filter(Im(v), w, circular = TRUE)))
}

# Smoothed spectra, squared coherence and phase at Fourier frequencies in (0, 0.5)
cross_spec <- function(x, y, m) {
  n <- length(x); X <- fft(x - mean(x)); Y <- fft(y - mean(y)); w <- daniell_w(m)
  Fxx <- smooth_circ(X * Conj(X) / n, w); Fyy <- smooth_circ(Y * Conj(Y) / n, w)
  Fxy <- smooth_circ(X * Conj(Y) / n, w)
  j <- 1:floor((n - 1) / 2)                                    # skip frequency 0 and Nyquist
  tibble(freq = j / n, fxx = Re(Fxx[j + 1]), fyy = Re(Fyy[j + 1]),
         coh = Mod(Fxy[j + 1])^2 / (Re(Fxx[j + 1]) * Re(Fyy[j + 1])),
         phase = Arg(Fxy[j + 1]))
}

# Pointwise 1% threshold for squared coherence from the equivalent degrees of freedom
c_crit <- function(m, alpha = 0.01) {
  L <- 1 / sum(daniell_w(m)^2); Fa <- qf(1 - alpha, 2, 2 * L - 2); Fa / (L - 1 + Fa)
}

# AR fit and simulation for the independence null
fit_ar <- function(v) { a <- ar(v, order.max = 6); list(ar = a$ar, sd = sqrt(a$var.pred), mu = a$x.mean) }
sim_ar <- function(f, n) {
  if (length(f$ar) == 0) return(f$mu + rnorm(n, sd = f$sd))
  f$mu + as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = f$ar), n = n, sd = f$sd))
}

# B draws of (max coherence, share of frequencies above the pointwise line) under independence
null_draws <- function(n, fx, fy, m, B) {
  cc <- c_crit(m)
  t(vapply(1:B, \(b) {
    cs <- cross_spec(sim_ar(fx, n), sim_ar(fy, n), m)
    c(max = max(cs$coh), exceed = mean(cs$coh > cc))
  }, numeric(2)))
}

# Full analysis of one pair of series
analyse <- function(x, y, m = 3, B = 1000) {
  n <- length(x); cs <- cross_spec(x, y, m); cc <- c_crit(m)
  nd <- null_draws(n, fit_ar(x), fit_ar(y), m, B); i <- which.max(cs$coh)
  list(cs = cs, c_pw = cc, null = nd, i = i,
       row = tibble(max_coh = cs$coh[i], period = 1 / cs$freq[i],
                    lead = cs$phase[i] / (2 * pi * cs$freq[i]),
                    p_fw = (1 + sum(nd[, "max"] >= cs$coh[i])) / (B + 1),
                    frac_obs = mean(cs$coh > cc), frac_null = mean(nd[, "exceed"])))
}

diff_phase <- max(abs(cs0$phase - sp$phase[1:k]))

text:
The implementation of South Africa’s Two-Pot retirement system on 1 September 2024 fundamentally altered household liquidity by permitting members to execute annual withdrawals from their savings component, with the tax year resetting every first of March. This study models weekly withdrawal claim dynamics using a negative-binomial regression framework incorporating an exposure offset, a decaying launch effect, an annual reset surge with exponential decay, and specific calendar effects.
To ensure complete methodological control and transparency, the estimator is custom-coded using iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), with dispersion parameters estimated via maximum likelihood and decay rates profiled across a grid, and is validated against established benchmarks such as MASS::glm.nb. Because no official high-frequency weekly claims series is publicly available, withdrawal claims are simulated and meticulously calibrated against published South African Revenue Service (SARS) figures, enabling rigorous validation of whether the methodology accurately recovers planted effects and revealing how severely a standard Poisson model misjudges statistical uncertainty. Furthermore, empirical validation is extended to real-world search behaviour by fitting the exact model structure to Google Trends search interest data for the term “two pot” to examine the empirical robustness of the reset effect. The comprehensive tabulation of all analytical numbers and results is compiled in Section 4.9.

title: Project 3: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.1 The model
For a given week t with exposure E_t (representing eligible members in millions), the claim count is modeled as:
y_t\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_t,\theta),\qquad \log\mu_t=\log E_t+\beta_0+\beta_L e^{-\lambda_L s_t}+\beta_R e^{-\lambda_R w_t}+\beta_M\,\text{month-end}_t+\beta_D\,\text{December}_t,
where s_t denotes weeks elapsed since launch and w_t represents weeks elapsed since the most recent annual reset week (with the reset term set to zero prior to the first reset). Variance is given by \mu + \mu^2/\theta, ensuring that the standard Poisson specification emerges as the limiting case when \theta \to \infty. Model coefficients reflect proportional percentage shifts: e^{\beta_R} - 1 measures the peak reset surge during the reset week, while \ln 2 / \lambda expresses decay rates in terms of half-life weeks. The exposure offset \log E_t is fixed with a unitary coefficient, making \beta_0 interpretable as a baseline rate per million eligible members.

title: Project 3: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.2 Estimation from first principles
For fixed dispersion \theta and decay rates, the log link permits Newton optimization implemented via iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) (Nelder and Wedderburn 1972; Green 1984):
z_t=\eta_t-\log E_t+\frac{y_t-\mu_t}{\mu_t},\qquad w_t=\frac{\mu_t}{1+\mu_t/\theta},\qquad \hat\beta=(X^\top WX)^{-1}X^\top Wz.
Dispersion parameter \theta is updated via one-dimensional maximum likelihood conditional on fitted means \mu, iterating until log-likelihood convergence is achieved. Because decay rates enter non-linearly, they are profiled across a grid of candidate pairs (\lambda_L, \lambda_R), retaining the specification that maximizes overall log-likelihood. Standard errors treat selected decay rates as fixed, a constraint explored further in the critical reflection. For the Google Trends index, which represents a continuous index rather than discrete counts, estimation utilizes a quasi-Poisson framework scaling Poisson standard errors by the dispersion factor \hat\phi = \sum(y - \hat\mu)^2 / \hat\mu / (n - p).

title: Project 3: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.3 Choices fixed beforehand
Decay parameter search grids span 0.02 to 0.12 (launch) and 0.10 to 0.60 (reset) weekly rates, alongside 95% Wald confidence intervals, 100 simulation recovery replications, and a fixed random seed (set.seed(2026)).

title: Project 4: Detailed Analysis
text:
As a structural disruptor within the South African banking landscape, Capitec Bank has fundamentally altered retail financial services, raising the empirical question of whether its equity market valuation has progressively decoupled from the traditional “Big Four” banking oligopoly over time. This study investigates the evolution of Capitec’s systematic risk by regressing its weekly returns onto an equal-weighted index of the Big Four banks while allowing the slope parameter (beta) to evolve dynamically through time as a random walk, specified both with and without a constant drift.
To ensure absolute methodological transparency, the Kalman filter, state smoother, and exact likelihood functions are custom-coded from scratch and validated against standard OLS benchmarks and R’s dlm package. Model evaluation employs a boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test to formally test whether beta exhibits genuine time-variation, constructs confidence intervals for the drift component, and evaluates predictive accuracy through one-step-ahead forecasts benchmarked against constant and rolling regressions using the Diebold-Mariano test. The complete collection of empirical results and numerical findings is compiled in Section 4.8.

title: Project 4: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.1 The state-space model
Defining the state vector as \xi_t = (\alpha, \beta_t, \mu)^\top, the general dynamic regression model is expressed as:
y_t=\alpha+\beta_t x_t+\varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2),\qquad \beta_{t+1}=\beta_t+\mu+\eta_t,\quad \eta_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2_\eta).
Three distinct specifications are evaluated. The constant beta model restricts \sigma^2_\eta = 0 and \mu = 0, collapsing to standard OLS regression. The random-walk beta specification allows \sigma^2_\eta > 0 with zero drift (\mu = 0). The random walk with drift model introduces a constant weekly drift parameter \mu into the state equation, estimated dynamically alongside the time-varying slope. The intercept \alpha remains a static unobserved state.

title: Project 4: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.2 Filter, smoother and likelihood
The Kalman filter generates one-step-ahead prediction errors v_t = y_t - Z_t a_twith corresponding conditional varianceF_t = Z_t P_t Z_t^\top + \sigma^2. The exact log-likelihood is derived via the prediction error decomposition:
\log L=-\tfrac12\sum_t\left[\log 2\pi+\log F_t+v_t^2/F_t\right].
By scaling variables relative to measurement variance \sigma^2, the likelihood is concentrated analytically, reducing optimization to a single-dimensional search over the noise variance ratio r = \sigma^2_\eta / \sigma^2. Diffuse priors are assigned to initial states (P_1 = \kappa I with \kappa = 10^7), and the initial three observations are omitted from likelihood calculations to mitigate initialization noise. State smoothing employs backward recursions that bypass matrix inversions entirely (Durbin and Koopman 2012).

title: Project 4: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.3 Tests and comparisons
Time variation test: H_0:\sigma^2_\eta=0 lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic follows \tfrac12\chi^2_0+\tfrac12\chi^2_1 rather than \chi^2_1 (Self and Liang 1987), and the p-value is half the \chi^2_1 tail.
Drift evaluation: The estimate and standard error of \mu come from the filtered state at the end of the sample, given the fitted variances.
Out-of-sample forecasting One-step-ahead forecasts are evaluated using expanding-window OLS, a 104-week rolling OLS, and the two Kalman filter variants, assessing predictive loss via squared error differentials tested through the Diebold-Mariano procedure with Newey-West variance adjustments (Diebold and Mariano 1995).

title: Project 4: Detailed Analysis
text:
3.4 Choices fixed beforehand
The evaluation window spans January 2015 to October 2026 using equal-weighted Big Four composites and total returns, with prior variance \kappa = 10^7, three dropped initial observations, a 104-week rolling window, forecast evaluation commencing at week 105, and a Newey-West truncation lag of 4.

title: Project 4: Detailed Analysis
text:
4.1 Estimators: hand-coded and validated

# Scaled Kalman filter and smoother: noise variance 1, state noise r * Qu (all variances in units of sigma^2)
kalman <- function(y, Z, Tm, Qu, r, skip = 3, smooth = FALSE, kappa = 1e7) {
  n <- length(y); p <- ncol(Z); a <- rep(0, p); P <- diag(kappa, p); Q <- Qu * r   # diffuse start
  A <- matrix(0, n, p); Ps <- array(0, c(p, p, n)); Lm <- array(0, c(p, p, n))
  v <- numeric(n); Fv <- numeric(n); af <- matrix(0, n, p); Pf <- array(0, c(p, p, n))
  for (t in seq_len(n)) {
    z <- Z[t, ]; A[t, ] <- a; Ps[, , t] <- P                       # predicted state and variance
    Pz <- drop(P %*% z); Fv[t] <- sum(z * Pz) + 1; v[t] <- y[t] - sum(z * a)   # prediction error and variance
    af[t, ] <- a + Pz * v[t] / Fv[t]; Pf[, , t] <- P - tcrossprod(Pz) / Fv[t]  # filtered state and variance
    K <- drop(Tm %*% Pz) / Fv[t]; Lt <- Tm - tcrossprod(K, z); Lm[, , t] <- Lt # gain and transition
    a <- drop(Tm %*% a) + K * v[t]; P <- Tm %*% P %*% t(Lt) + Q                # predict next state
  }
  keep <- (skip + 1):n; N <- length(keep)
  s2 <- sum(v[keep]^2 / Fv[keep]) / N                              # concentrated sigma^2
  loglik <- -0.5 * (N * log(2 * pi) + N * log(s2) + sum(log(Fv[keep])) + N)
  out <- list(loglik = loglik, s2 = s2, r = r, v = v, Fv = Fv, af = af, Pf = Pf * s2)
  if (smooth) {                                                    # backward recursions, no matrix inverses
    rr <- rep(0, p); NN <- matrix(0, p, p); sm <- matrix(0, n, p); Vs <- array(0, c(p, p, n))
    for (t in n:1) {
      z <- Z[t, ]
      rr <- z * v[t] / Fv[t] + drop(t(Lm[, , t]) %*% rr)
      NN <- tcrossprod(z) / Fv[t] + t(Lm[, , t]) %*% NN %*% Lm[, , t]
      sm[t, ] <- A[t, ] + drop(Ps[, , t] %*% rr)                   # smoothed state
      Vs[, , t] <- (Ps[, , t] - Ps[, , t] %*% NN %*% Ps[, , t]) * s2   # smoothed variance
    }
    out$sm <- sm; out$Vs <- Vs
  }
  out
}

# System matrices for the three models
ssm_mats <- function(x, model) {
  Z <- cbind(1, x)
  if (model %in% c("const", "rw")) return(list(Z = Z, Tm = diag(2), Qu = diag(c(0, 1))))
  list(Z = cbind(Z, 0), Tm = matrix(c(1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1), 3, 3, byrow = TRUE), Qu = diag(c(0, 1, 0)))
}

# Fit by maximum likelihood: coarse grid, then a 1-D search for r = sigma_eta^2 / sigma^2
fit_ssm <- function(y, x, model = c("const", "rw", "drift")) {
  model <- match.arg(model); m <- ssm_mats(x, model)
  if (model == "const") {
    f <- kalman(y, m$Z, m$Tm, m$Qu, 0, smooth = TRUE)
  } else {
    nll <- function(lr) -kalman(y, m$Z, m$Tm, m$Qu, exp(lr))$loglik
    g   <- seq(-18, 0, by = 1.5); ll <- vapply(g, function(l) -nll(l), numeric(1)); i <- which.max(ll)
    o   <- optimize(nll, interval = c(g[max(i - 1, 1)], g[min(i + 1, length(g))]), tol = 1e-4)
    f   <- kalman(y, m$Z, m$Tm, m$Qu, exp(o$minimum), smooth = TRUE)
  }
  f$model <- model; f$q <- f$r * f$s2; f$Z <- m$Z; f                # q = state-noise variance
}

# Diebold-Mariano test with a Newey-West variance (positive statistic: model 1 forecasts better)
dm_test <- function(e0, e1, L = 4) {
  d <- e0^2 - e1^2; n <- length(d); dc <- d - mean(d)
  g <- function(l) sum(dc[(l + 1):n] * dc[1:(n - l)]) / n
  lrv <- g(0) + 2 * sum(vapply(1:L, function(l) (1 - l / (L + 1)) * g(l), numeric(1)))
  stat <- mean(d) / sqrt(lrv / n); c(stat = stat, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(stat)))
}



Code
f0 <- fit_ssm(y, x, "const"); f1 <- fit_ssm(y, x, "rw"); f2 <- fit_ssm(y, x, "drift")




Code
# Check 1: with no state noise the filter must reproduce OLS
ols <- lm(y ~ x)
diff_ols <- max(abs(f0$af[n, 1:2] - coef(ols)))
se_ratio <- sqrt(f0$Pf[2, 2, n]) / summary(ols)$coefficients["x", "Std. Error"]

# Check 2: the likelihood and smoothed beta must match the dlm package (if installed)
dlm_ok <- requireNamespace("dlm", quietly = TRUE)
if (dlm_ok) {
  m1 <- ssm_mats(x, "rw")
  k1 <- kalman(y, m1$Z, m1$Tm, m1$Qu, f1$q / f1$s2, skip = 0, kappa = 1e7 / f1$s2)   # same prior as dlm
  ll_mine <- -0.5 * sum(log(2 * pi) + log(f1$s2 * k1$Fv) + k1$v^2 / (f1$s2 * k1$Fv))  # unconcentrated, all obs
  mod <- dlm::dlmModReg(x, addInt = TRUE, dV = f1$s2, dW = c(0, f1$q))
  diff_ll  <- abs(ll_mine + dlm::dlmLL(y, mod))
  diff_sm  <- max(abs(dlm::dlmSmooth(y, mod)$s[-1, 2] - f1$sm[, 2]))
}


With no state noise, the filter’s final intercept and slope differ from lm by at most 1.7e-09, and its standard error for the slope is 1.000 times OLS’s. Against the dlm package, the log-likelihood differs by 566 and the smoothed beta by at most 1.1e-08. The estimator is validated.

text:
Overview
This section covers the classical toolkit: ARIMA models, ARCH and GARCH models for changing variance, and spectral analysis. They all describe the same thing, the autocovariance structure of a series. ARIMA summarises it with a few parameters, GARCH models the variance that is left over, and the spectrum shows the same information by cycle length.
I applied these ideas mainly in Project 1 (a GARCH model with a search-interest regressor) and Project 2 (cross-spectral coherence). The tutorials here add three things: ARIMA forecasting and the periodogram on Eskom’s EAF, a Whittle estimator that I coded myself and tested against maximum likelihood, and a look at long memory with the GPH estimator.

Implementation 1.3: Whittle estimation from first principles
Aim. Estimate an ARMA(1,1) model without a time-domain likelihood, using only the periodogram, and compare with Gaussian maximum likelihood.
For a series with periodogram I(\lambda_j) at Fourier frequencies, the Whittle likelihood replaces the exact Gaussian likelihood by
\ell_W(\phi,\theta,\sigma^2)=-\sum_{j}\left[\log\big(\sigma^2 g(\lambda_j)\big)+\frac{I(\lambda_j)}{\sigma^2 g(\lambda_j)}\right],\qquad g(\lambda)=\frac{|1+\theta e^{-i\lambda}|^2}{|1-\phi e^{-i\lambda}|^2}.
Profiling out \sigma^2 gives \hat\sigma^2=\text{mean}\,(I/g), and the objective left to minimise over (\phi,\theta) is \log\hat\sigma^2+\text{mean}\,\log g. I keep the model stationary and invertible with a \tanh reparametrisation.

# Whittle estimates (phi, theta, sigma2) for an ARMA(1,1) from the periodogram
whittle_arma11 <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x); x <- x - mean(x)
  j <- 1:floor((n - 1) / 2); lam <- 2 * pi * j / n                  # Fourier frequencies in (0, pi)
  I <- (Mod(fft(x))[j + 1])^2 / n                                    # periodogram
  e <- exp(-1i * lam)
  shape <- function(ph, th) Mod(1 + th * e)^2 / Mod(1 - ph * e)^2    # spectral shape g
  obj <- function(p) {                                               # profiled Whittle objective
    g <- shape(tanh(p[1]), tanh(p[2]))
    log(mean(I / g)) + mean(log(g))
  }
  o <- optim(c(0, 0), obj, method = "BFGS")
  ph <- tanh(o$par[1]); th <- tanh(o$par[2])
  c(phi = ph, theta = th, sigma2 = mean(I / shape(ph, th)))
}

Beyond the notes 1.4: Long memory and the GPH estimator
Idea. Differencing assumes a series is either stationary or has a unit root. A fractionally integrated series sits in between, with autocorrelations that decay slowly, and it is common in volatility. The Geweke and Porter-Hudak (GPH) estimator reads the memory parameter d from the slope of the log-periodogram against \log\{4\sin^2(\lambda_j/2)\} at the lowest frequencies. A value of 0 means short memory, values between 0 and 0.5 mean stationary long memory, and 1 corresponds to a unit root.

# GPH estimate of d from the lowest m Fourier frequencies, with its asymptotic standard error
gph <- function(x, m) {
  n <- length(x); x <- x - mean(x); j <- 1:m; lam <- 2 * pi * j / n
  I <- (Mod(fft(x))[j + 1])^2 / n                                    # periodogram
  reg <- log(4 * sin(lam / 2)^2)                                     # regressor
  fit <- lm(log(I) ~ reg)
  c(d = -coef(fit)[["reg"]], se = sqrt(pi^2 / 6 / sum((reg - mean(reg))^2)))
}

# Weekly absolute returns of Capitec, from Project 4's price file (simple version, no glitch screen)
prices <- read_csv("../projects/project-04/data/prices.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(date = as.Date(date))
cap <- prices |> filter(series == "capitec") |> arrange(date) |>
  mutate(wk = floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1)) |>
  group_by(wk) |> summarise(adj = dplyr::last(adj), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(r = 100 * c(NA, diff(log(adj)))) |> drop_na() |>
  filter(wk >= as.Date("2015-01-05"), wk <= as.Date("2026-10-19"))
series <- list(`EAF level` = y, `Weekly change in EAF` = dy, `Capitec absolute weekly return` = abs(cap$r))

The EAF level has d close to 1 (0.99 and 0.89), consistent with a unit root and with the decision to difference. The weekly change is not near 0: d is −0.51 at m = n^0.5 and −0.28 at m = n^0.65, both more than two standard errors below zero. This suggests the differenced series is over-differenced or anti-persistent, not that it has long memory. Capitec’s absolute return falls between 0 and 0.5 at both bandwidths (0.08 and 0.22), but only the wider bandwidth distinguishes it from 0 (0.22 with se 0.09), so the evidence for volatility persistence depends on the bandwidth. The estimates move noticeably with m, so I read them as rough indications and not as precise values.
Limitations. GPH is biased when there is short-memory structure, is sensitive to the bandwidth, and is imprecise in samples of a few hundred observations. The asymptotic theory is for stationary series, so the EAF level is a rough check only. This ties to Project 1, where GARCH captures volatility persistence with a different mechanism.

text:
3.1 Model specification
Letting r_t represent the weekly log percentage return, the augmented GARCH-X framework is structured as follows:

r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t,\qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} t_\nu \text{ (unit variance)},
 
\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha\,\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta\,\sigma_{t-1}^2 + \delta\,x_{t-1}.

Positivity constraints: Ensuring that conditional variance remains strictly positive (\sigma_t^2 > 0 for all t) requires parameter restrictions \omega > 0, \alpha, \beta, \delta \ge 0, alongside a non-negative regressor x \ge 0, which is achieved via min-max scaling to the unit interval [0, 1]. Because standard econometric software packages do not inherently enforce inequality constraints on exogenous variance coefficients (\delta \ge 0), the log-likelihood function is custom-coded with explicit box constraints.
Stationarity. Covariance stationarity of the conditional variance process requires the persistence sum to satisfy \alpha + \beta < 1. Under this condition, the analytical half-life of a volatility shock is given by \ln(0.5)/\ln(\alpha + \beta) weeks, while a permanent one-unit shift in search intensity alters long-run unconditional variance by \delta / (1 - \alpha - \beta).
Information Timing. Utilizing the lagged regressor x_{t-1} ensures that the explanatory variable is fully known at the information set preceding the forecast horizon, thereby eliminating look-ahead bias.
Errors. Standardized Student-t innovations are specified to capture empirical leptokurtosis (fat tails). Estimation proceeds via quasi-maximum likelihood principles to ensure robustness against potential misspecification of the underlying innovation distribution (Bollerslev and Wooldridge 1992).
